newsitem.title: IRAQ: Kurds flee embattled north Iraq by the thousands.
newsitem.headline: Kurds flee embattled north Iraq by the thousands.

text.p: Thousands of Kurds have fled from embattled northern Iraq in cars, trucks and even bulldozers after a Baghdad-backed Kurdish faction seized two strategic towns in heavy fighting.
The refugees raced towards Iran after forces of the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) captured the towns from the rival Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) on Sunday.
The United States warned Baghdad it would not hesitate to strike against any Iraqi aggression but said it could not confirm reports of an Iraqi role in the fresh Kurdish fighting.
The village of Degala was the first to fall to the KDP. Hours later the Iraqi-backed group also seized Koi Sanjaq, a city of 80,000.
Koi Sanjaq, 100 km (65 miles) northwest of Sulaimaniya, is the PUK's last remaining stronghold in the Iraqi north.
PUK commanders said on Saturday that Iraq had moved tanks into a position that would place Sulaimaniya under attack from three fronts.
The PUK said that it came under heavy artillery and tank fire from combined Iraqi and KDP forces in Sunday's attacks.
The PUK guerrillas appealed to the United States for help, saying Washington should strike again at Iraqi President Saddam Hussein.
"Urgent and decisive help is needed. We call on the U.S.-led coalition to move urgently to stop the Iraqi onslaught," the PUK said in a statement.
American forces last week fired 44 cruise missiles on southern Iraq to retaliate for what it said was Saddam's role in helping the KDP seize the PUK-held town of Arbil.

But U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said Washington had no evidence of a major Iraqi role in the latest Kurdish factional fighting. He referred to the Kurdish fighting as a civil war and said it would be a mistake for the United States to intervene.
Sunday's clashes on Sunday followed several days of fierce fighting between the rival Kurdish militias battling to control predominantly Kurdish northern Iraq.
PUK commanders said their commander-in-chief, Jalal Talabani, had joined his fighters at Heibet Sultan, a 200-metre- high mountain and the PUK's next line of defence after Koi Sanjaq.
"There is nothing so natural as the head commander's coming to the battleground," said a local PUK commander.
But a spokesman at KDP headquarters in Salahuddin said later that the KDP had also taken the mountain. He said there were hundreds of PUK dead, wounded and captured but had no further details.
